Brody New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Lviv Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Brody's new Jewish cemetery was established in the 1830s by decree of the Austrian government following a cholera epidemic, replacing an older cemetery; it is considered one of the most beautiful and best-preserved 19th-century Jewish cemeteries in Ukraine, renowned for its stone carvings and poetic epitaphs. Jews were the majority population from the city's founding in the late 16th century, surviving the plague, the 1648 Khmelnytsky massacre, and a 1651 Tatar invasion, and later grew to as much as 88 percent of the town by 1820. Brody's main religious circles initially resisted both Hasidism and the more heterodox Sabbatean and Frankist movements, though Hasidic ideas eventually took hold and the city became a center of both Galician Hasidism and the Haskalah; Nachman Krochmal, a leading Haskalah figure born in Brody in 1785, later lived and worked in Ternopil, documented elsewhere in this collection. A ghetto holding 6,458 Jews was established here in January 1942, and about 3,000 were deported to the Bełżec death camp later that year; only about 250 Jews returned after the war.
